lines.s10: Glera is the grape of Prosecco: light, bright bubbles that taste of green apple, pear and white peach.
lines.s20: Glera is the grape behind Prosecco, from the hills north of Venice. It makes a light sparkling wine of green apple, pear and acacia blossom, soft and easy from the first sip.
lines.s45: Glera is the grape of Prosecco, grown in the Veneto and Friuli in the north east of Italy. It tastes of green apple, ripe pear and white peach, with a scent of acacia blossom. The wine is light in body and gentle in alcohol, and often just off dry. Its bubbles are made in a sealed tank, not in the bottle, which keeps that fresh fruit in front. Champagne tastes of bread and time, and Prosecco tastes of the grape. Pour it before dinner, with cured ham and melon, or with anything fried. Until 2009 the grape itself was called Prosecco, and the name now belongs to the place.
lines.sale: Glera, as Prosecco, is the easy way to begin: green apple, pear and soft bubbles that ask nothing of you. I would open the evening with it, beside the fried seafood or the ham.

glass.lead: Green apple, ripe pear and white peach with acacia blossom, light and fresh, often with a touch of sweetness.

ladder.where: The steep hills of Conegliano Valdobbiadene and Asolo
The plains of the Veneto and Friuli

glass.structure: Dry to off dry, with medium plus acidity, a light body and moderate alcohol; a soft, frothy sparkle.

home.home: The north east of Italy: the Veneto and Friuli Venezia Giulia under the name Prosecco, with the steep hills of Conegliano Valdobbiadene and Asolo at its heart. The second fermentation happens in a sealed tank, so the wine keeps its green apple and pear freshness and is sold young.
home.abroad: It rarely leaves home. Australia grows it and still calls the grape Prosecco, a name Europe keeps for the Italian zone, so a bottle labelled Glera is seldom seen.

service.temp: 43 to 46 degrees Fahrenheit, 6 to 8 degrees Celsius, straight from the ice bucket.
service.glass: A tulip shaped sparkling glass or a white wine glass; a narrow flute hides the perfume.
service.decant: No. Open it cold and pour gently in two motions to keep the sparkle.
service.age: Enjoy it young, within a year or two of release; freshness is the point.

with.why: soft fruit and bubbles against salt and sweetness
bubbles and acidity cut through the frying
a touch of sweetness cools the mustard and cayenne
a gentle wine that does not crowd the plate

labels.means: A place name since 2009, not a grape: sparkling Glera from the Veneto and Friuli.
Sweeter than Brut, not drier: a soft, slightly sweet style long traditional for Prosecco.
Spumante is fully sparkling; Frizzante is gently sparkling, with a softer fizz.
The steep hill zone, labelled Prosecco Superiore; Rive names a single hillside village, Cartizze one prized hill.
Refermented in the bottle and sold cloudy, on its yeast.

guest.q: Is Prosecco the same thing as Champagne?
guest.a: No. Champagne is from France, from other grapes, and gets its bubbles in the bottle, which gives bread and toast. Prosecco is Glera from Italy, made in a tank to keep its fresh apple and pear.

guest.q: I asked for a dry one. Why does Extra Dry taste a little sweet?
guest.a: The names run backwards. Brut is the drier style and Extra Dry carries a little more sugar, so ask for Brut if you want it crisp.

guest.q: The label only says Prosecco. What is Glera?
guest.a: Glera is the grape. It was itself called Prosecco until 2009, when the name was kept for the place and its wines.

compare.tell: Chardonnay in Champagne gives lemon, chalk and brioche from years on its lees; Glera stays with green apple, pear and acacia blossom, lighter and softer.
Macabeo leads Cava, which is made in the bottle like Champagne and tastes drier, with toast and almond; Glera is softer and more openly fruity.
Moscato d'Asti is sweeter, lower in alcohol and loudly grapey, with orange blossom; Glera is drier and far quieter in scent.

profile.st: Pale straw with a fine, frothy mousse · Body light · Acid medium plus · Alcohol low to moderate · Dry to off dry, usually sparkling
profile.fruit: Green apple, ripe pear, white peach; yellow apple and apricot from warmer sites
profile.other: Acacia blossom, wisteria and honeysuckle; little yeast character, since the bubbles are made in a tank; often a touch of sweetness
profile.tell: Light and softly sparkling, with green apple, pear and acacia blossom and no bready note: tank method fruit, not bottle age
profile.regions: Prosecco in the Veneto and Friuli Venezia Giulia; Conegliano Valdobbiadene and Asolo in the hills
profile.confuse: Champagne and Cava show brioche and toast from bottle ageing; Moscato d'Asti is sweeter and more grapey; Glera sits between, fresh and scented with acacia

cards.front: Glera: which wine does it make, and how are the bubbles made?
cards.back: Prosecco, from the Veneto and Friuli Venezia Giulia. The second fermentation takes place in a sealed tank, the Martinotti or Charmat method, which keeps the fruit fresh.

cards.front: On a Prosecco label, which is sweeter: Brut or Extra Dry?
cards.back: Extra Dry. Brut holds less than 12 grams of sugar a litre; Extra Dry holds 12 to 17, and Dry 17 to 32.

cards.front: How much Glera must a Prosecco hold, and what happened in 2009?
cards.back: At least 85 per cent. In 2009 the grape, until then called Prosecco, was renamed Glera, and Prosecco became a protected place name.

questions.q: A guest wants bubbles with no hint of sweetness, and the list offers one Prosecco in four styles. Which do you pour?
questions.exp: Of the four, Brut holds the least sugar, under 12 grams a litre. Extra Dry and Dry are both sweeter than Brut, despite their names, and Demi-Sec is sweeter still.

questions.q: A sparkling wine poured blind is pale, light and softly fizzy, all green apple, pear and acacia blossom, with no bread or toast. Which is it most likely to be?
questions.exp: Green apple, pear and acacia with no bready note point to the tank method and Glera. Champagne, Cava and Franciacorta are made in the bottle and show brioche or toast.

questions.q: A guest asks why the front label says Prosecco and the back label says Glera. What is the difference?
opts: Prosecco is the place and the wine; Glera is the grape
Glera is the village; Prosecco is the grape
Prosecco is sparkling; Glera is the still version
Glera is a sweeter style of Prosecco
questions.exp: Since 2009 Prosecco has been a protected place name for wines of the Veneto and Friuli Venezia Giulia, and the grape, once called Prosecco too, is Glera.
